parts.title: 大問1 短文の語句空所補充
parts.desc: 1〜2文の空所に入る難しい単語・句動詞を4つから選ぶ
parts.tip: まず文全体を読み、空所の語が「良い意味か悪い意味か」「強めか弱めか」を決める。セミコロンや because・although の後ろが言い換えの手がかり。知らない語は接頭辞（in- / dis- / ex-）と語根から消去法で絞る。
parts.intro: Read each sentence and choose the word or phrase from the four choices that best completes it.

questions.q: The committee's report was so ____ that even experts struggled to follow it; its main arguments were buried under pages of technical detail and unexplained abbreviations.
choices: candid
frugal
placid
abstruse
questions.why: abstruse＝「難解な」。専門家でも追えない、細部と略語に埋もれている、という説明と合う。candid（率直な）、frugal（質素な）、placid（穏やかな）は報告書の分かりにくさを表さない。

questions.q: After months of negotiation, the two firms finally signed a deal, but analysts warned that the ____ agreement could collapse if either side changed its priorities.
choices: lucid
tenuous
opulent
verbose
questions.why: tenuous＝「もろい・根拠の弱い」。どちらかの方針が変われば崩れかねない、という警告と合う。lucid（明快な）、opulent（豪華な）、verbose（言葉数の多い）は「崩れやすさ」を表さない。

questions.q: The novelist was famously ____ in interviews, often answering long questions with a single word and refusing to discuss anything about her private life.
choices: gregarious
voracious
taciturn
pliant
questions.why: taciturn＝「無口な」。長い質問に一語で答える、私生活を話さない、と合う。gregarious（社交的な）は逆。voracious（貪欲な）、pliant（従順な）は合わない。

questions.q: Dr. Hale tried to ____ his theory with data from three separate studies, but critics argued that the samples were far too small to prove anything.
choices: obfuscate
relinquish
corroborate
castigate
questions.why: corroborate＝「（証拠で）裏付ける」。3つの研究のデータで、しかし標本が小さすぎて証明にならない、と続く。obfuscate（わざと分かりにくくする）、relinquish（手放す）、castigate（厳しく非難する）は合わない。

questions.q: Although the union leader seemed ____ at first, refusing to consider any form of compromise, he eventually agreed to a modest pay increase for workers.
choices: magnanimous
intransigent
ebullient
gullible
questions.why: intransigent＝「妥協しない・頑固な」。どんな妥協も拒む、と言い換えている。magnanimous（寛大な）は逆。ebullient（元気あふれる）、gullible（だまされやすい）は合わない。

questions.q: Heavy snow ____ the climbers' progress throughout the afternoon, and they reached the mountain hut nearly three hours later than they had planned.
choices: enunciated
exonerated
impeded
emulated
questions.why: impede＝「妨げる・遅らせる」。雪のせいで3時間遅れた、という結果と合う。enunciate（はっきり発音する）、exonerate（無実を証明する）、emulate（見習う）は合わない。

questions.q: Paul's apology struck his colleagues as ____; he had made exactly the same promise twice before and had never actually changed his behavior.
choices: disingenuous
indelible
impeccable
incessant
questions.why: disingenuous＝「不誠実な・本心でない」。同じ約束を2回破っている、という根拠と合う。indelible（消えない）、impeccable（非の打ちどころがない）、incessant（絶え間ない）は合わない。

questions.q: Years of ____ spending left the family with almost no savings, so they were forced to sell their vacation home when Mr. Lowe lost his job.
choices: austere
tacit
nascent
profligate
questions.why: profligate＝「浪費的な」。貯金がほとんど無くなった原因になる。austere（切り詰めた）は逆。tacit（暗黙の）、nascent（生まれたばかりの）は spending を説明しない。

questions.q: The professor's lecture contained several ____ remarks about rival researchers, and a number of students later complained that the comments had been unprofessional.
choices: disparaging
exculpatory
conciliatory
salubrious
questions.why: disparaging＝「見くびった・けなすような」。学生がプロらしくないと苦情を言った、と合う。exculpatory（無罪を示す）、conciliatory（なだめるような）、salubrious（健康に良い）は合わない。

questions.q: When the company's sales began to ____ last year, the board replaced the chief executive and announced an ambitious plan to enter overseas markets.
choices: coalesce
reverberate
germinate
dwindle
questions.why: dwindle＝「次第に減る」。社長交代と海外進出の計画、という立て直しの対応と合う。coalesce（合体する）、reverberate（反響する）、germinate（発芽する）は売上に使わない。

questions.q: The mediator managed to ____ the tension in the room by making a joke about the broken air conditioner, and the talks continued calmly after that.
choices: exacerbate
emancipate
encapsulate
defuse
questions.why: defuse＝「（緊張・危機を）和らげる」。冗談の後、話し合いが落ち着いて続いた。exacerbate（悪化させる）は逆。emancipate（解放する）、encapsulate（要約する）は合わない。

questions.q: The documentary was criticized for its ____ treatment of a complex scientific debate, presenting only one side and ignoring decades of contrary evidence.
choices: tendentious
meticulous
venerable
sonorous
questions.why: tendentious＝「偏った・特定の主張に肩入れした」。一方の側だけを見せ、反対の証拠を無視した。meticulous（細心の）、venerable（尊い）、sonorous（よく響く）は批判の理由にならない。

questions.q: The hotel's ____ lobby, with its marble floors, crystal chandeliers, and gold-framed mirrors, impressed guests the moment they walked through the doors.
choices: opulent
dilapidated
austere
rudimentary
questions.why: opulent＝「豪華な」。大理石の床・シャンデリア・金縁の鏡、という例と合う。dilapidated（荒れ果てた）、austere（簡素な）、rudimentary（初歩的な）は逆の印象。

questions.q: Although Mr. Grant had ____ his support for the project at the first meeting, he changed his mind after reading the final budget and voted against it.
choices: dispelled
abdicated
extricated
avowed
questions.why: avow＝「公言する」。最初は支持を表明 → 予算を見て反対、という Although の対比。dispel（払いのける）、abdicate（退位する・放棄する）、extricate（救い出す）は support と組まない。

questions.q: Dr. Moreno was ____ by her failed experiments; instead of giving up, she redesigned her equipment and began a new series of trials the following week.
choices: undaunted
incensed
belittled
encumbered
questions.why: undaunted＝「ひるまない」。あきらめずに翌週また始めた、と合う。incensed（激怒した）、belittled（けなされた）、encumbered（重荷を負った）は instead of giving up とつながらない。

questions.q: Critics ____ the director for casting inexperienced actors in the main roles, saying that their stiff performances ruined an otherwise excellent script.
choices: commended
vindicated
lambasted
placated
questions.why: lambaste＝「酷評する」。演技が脚本を台無しにした、という批判と合う。commend（ほめる）は逆。vindicate（正しさを証明する）、placate（なだめる）も合わない。

questions.q: To ____ the risk of mold, the museum keeps its rare manuscripts in special rooms where both the temperature and the humidity are carefully controlled.
choices: aggravate
mitigate
emulate
extrapolate
questions.why: mitigate＝「（危険・害を）和らげる」。温度と湿度を管理するのはカビの危険を減らすため。aggravate（悪化させる）は逆。emulate（見習う）、extrapolate（推定する）は合わない。

questions.q: Jenny's ____ curiosity led her to read everything she could find about deep-sea creatures, from picture books for children to graduate-level textbooks.
choices: impassive
insatiable
infallible
innocuous
questions.why: insatiable＝「飽くことのない」。見つけた物は絵本から大学院の教科書まで全部読んだ。impassive（無表情な）、infallible（絶対に誤らない）、innocuous（無害な）は好奇心の強さを表さない。

questions.q: The economist's model rested on a ____ assumption: that all consumers behave rationally, an idea that research in psychology has repeatedly shown to be false.
choices: sanguine
opportune
fallacious
palatable
questions.why: fallacious＝「誤った」。心理学の研究で何度も否定された、と続く。sanguine（楽観的な）、opportune（時宜を得た）、palatable（口に合う・受け入れやすい）は「誤り」の意味にならない。

questions.q: After the factory closed, the once-busy town fell into a long period of economic ____, with shops boarded up and young people moving away.
choices: proliferation
exuberance
malaise
remuneration
questions.why: malaise＝「（経済などの）不振・沈滞」。店が閉まり若者が出て行く様子と合う。proliferation（急増）、exuberance（活気）、remuneration（報酬）は合わない。

questions.q: The company tried to ____ public criticism of its new product by offering free repairs, but many customers had already switched to rival brands.
choices: incite
exalt
emanate
deflect
questions.why: deflect criticism＝「批判をかわす」。無料修理という対策と合う。incite（あおる）は逆。exalt（称える）、emanate（発する。自動詞）は合わない。

questions.q: Engineers spent several weeks trying to ____ the cause of the software failure, eventually tracing it to a single line of outdated code.
choices: ameliorate
promulgate
ascertain
recuperate
questions.why: ascertain＝「（事実を）突き止める」。原因を探し、1行のコードにたどり着いた。ameliorate（改善する）、promulgate（公布する）、recuperate（回復する）は the cause と組まない。

questions.q: Many first-time visitors find the old city's ____ alleyways confusing; without a good map, it is easy to walk in circles for an hour or more.
choices: pristine
sedentary
labyrinthine
perennial
questions.why: labyrinthine＝「迷路のような」。地図が無いと同じ所を回ってしまう、と合う。pristine（汚れていない）、sedentary（座りがちな）、perennial（長年続く）は道を説明しない。

questions.q: Although the position was ____, offering a high salary and generous annual bonuses, Kenji resigned after a year because he found the work unfulfilling.
choices: lucrative
frivolous
ominous
clandestine
questions.why: lucrative＝「もうかる」。高い給料とボーナス、と言い換えている。frivolous（軽薄な）、ominous（不吉な）、clandestine（秘密の）は給料の良さを表さない。

questions.q: The young biologist's findings were ____ by many of her peers at first, but within a decade her theory had become widely accepted in the field.
choices: lauded
derided
augmented
annexed
questions.why: deride＝「あざける・ばかにする」。but 以下の「後に広く受け入れられた」と対比になる。lauded（称賛された）では対比にならない。augmented（増やされた）、annexed（併合された）は合わない。

questions.q: The guide warned the tourists that the river was ____ in several places and told them not to cross without holding firmly onto the rope.
choices: placid
treacherous
arid
docile
questions.why: treacherous＝「（見かけによらず）危険な」。ロープにつかまって渡れ、という警告と合う。placid（穏やかな）は逆。arid（乾燥した）、docile（おとなしい）も合わない。

questions.q: The two firms decided to ____ their research departments, hoping that combining their expertise would speed up the development of new medicines.
choices: fragment
amalgamate
emancipate
decimate
questions.why: amalgamate＝「合併する・統合する」。combining their expertise（専門知識を合わせる）と同じ意味。fragment（分割する）は逆。emancipate（解放する）、decimate（大量に減らす）は合わない。

questions.q: The old theater was ____ with mice that had nested inside its walls, so the owners closed it for several weeks while pest-control workers dealt with the problem.
choices: infested
imbued
endowed
adorned
questions.why: be infested with ～＝「（害虫などが）はびこっている」。駆除の間閉館した。imbued（染み込んだ）、endowed（恵まれた）、adorned（飾られた）は害のある物には使わない。

questions.q: Rachel's ____ comments about the new logo hurt her colleague's feelings, though she later insisted that she had only been trying to be honest.
choices: benign
effusive
cordial
caustic
questions.why: caustic＝「辛辣な」。相手を傷つけた、正直に言っただけだと弁解した、と合う。benign（優しい）、cordial（心のこもった）は逆。effusive（感情をあふれさせた・大げさにほめる）も人を傷つけない。

questions.q: Ms. Rivera was ____ to accept the promotion at first, worried that the extra responsibilities would leave her very little time for her young family.
choices: privy
akin
rife
loath
questions.why: be loath to do＝「～するのに気が進まない」。家族との時間が減るのを心配した。privy to（～を内々に知る）、akin to（～に似た）、rife with（～だらけの）は後ろに動詞の原形を取れない。

questions.q: The small bakery has developed a ____ following; on weekends, customers line up outside before dawn to buy its famous sourdough bread.
choices: fleeting
fervent
nominal
desultory
questions.why: fervent＝「熱烈な」。夜明け前から並ぶ客、という例と合う。fleeting（つかの間の）、nominal（名ばかりの）、desultory（気まぐれな）は熱心さと逆の意味。

questions.q: Because the instructions were so ____, half of the participants misunderstood what they were supposed to do and had to repeat the experiment.
choices: nebulous
explicit
punctual
prolific
questions.why: nebulous＝「あいまいな・漠然とした」。半数が誤解した原因になる。explicit（明確な）は逆。punctual（時間を守る）、prolific（多作の）は指示を説明しない。

questions.q: The chef's new menu was a ____ success; within a month, reservations had doubled and critics were praising it in several national magazines.
choices: marginal
resounding
specious
perfunctory
questions.why: a resounding success＝「大成功」。予約が倍、全国誌でほめられた。marginal（わずかな）、perfunctory（おざなりの）は成功の大きさを表さない。specious（もっともらしいがうそっぽい）も合わない。

questions.q: The sale of the house almost ____ when the buyer discovered serious problems with the roof, but the owner agreed to lower the price by ten percent.
choices: drew up
set off
fell through
turned in
questions.why: fall through＝「（計画・取引が）だめになる」。屋根の問題で売買が流れかけた → 値下げで助かった。draw up（作成する）、set off（出発する）、turn in（提出する・寝る）は合わない。

questions.q: Mark's parents told him he could not keep ____ his decision about which university to attend, since the application deadline was only a week away.
choices: bringing about
running over
handing out
putting off
questions.why: put off＝「先延ばしにする」。締め切りが1週間後なので、決断を延ばせない。bring about（引き起こす）、run over（ひく・ざっと見直す）、hand out（配る）は合わない。

questions.q: The excitement over the new phone soon ____ when users discovered that its battery lasted only half a day and that the camera often froze.
choices: chipped in
wore off
stood out
pulled through
questions.why: wear off＝「（効果・感情が）薄れる」。電池が半日しかもたないと分かり、熱が冷めた。chip in（お金を出し合う）、stand out（目立つ）、pull through（切り抜ける）は合わない。

questions.q: After working for a large bakery chain for twelve years, Alan finally had enough savings to ____ on his own and open a small shop downtown.
choices: strike out
bear out
pore over
fend off
questions.why: strike out on one's own＝「独立する」。大手を辞めて自分の店を開く。bear out（裏付ける）、pore over（熟読する）、fend off（撃退する）は on one's own と組まない。

questions.q: The speaker ____ on minor details of the project's history for so long that she had no time left to explain its most important results.
choices: embarked
reneged
encroached
dwelt
questions.why: dwell on ～＝「～についてくどくど話す」。細かい話に時間を使い、肝心の結果を話す時間が無くなった。embark on（乗り出す）、renege on（約束を破る）、encroach on（侵害する）は合わない。

questions.q: The marketing team had to ____ a completely new campaign in just two days after the original one was canceled at the last minute.
choices: throw together
write off
stave off
look down
questions.why: throw together＝「急ごしらえで作る」。2日で新しいキャンペーンを作った。write off（帳消しにする・見切る）、stave off（食い止める）、look down（見下ろす）は合わない。

questions.q: When the hikers ran out of food on the third day, they had to ____ on the few energy bars that one member had packed at the bottom of his bag.
choices: cash in
hold out
fall back
chime in
questions.why: fall back on ～＝「（いざという時に）～に頼る」。食料が尽きて、残りの栄養バーに頼った。cash in on（～で利益を得る）、hold out on（～に隠し事をする）、chime in（口をはさむ）は合わない。

parts.title: 大問2 長文の語句空所補充
parts.desc: 約350語の説明文・評論文の空所3つに入る語句を4つから選ぶ
parts.tip: 空所の後ろの1〜2文（具体例・言い換え）が根拠になることが多い。段落の頭の空所は「前の段落と逆か・続きか」を先に決める。選択肢は本文の語を使った引っかけが多いので、意味で選ぶ。
parts.intro: Read each passage and choose the best phrase from among the four choices for each numbered blank.

sets.passage:
Too Many Choices?

For decades, economists took it for granted that having more options could only benefit consumers. If a shopper finds a selection too large, the reasoning went, she can simply ignore the items that do not interest her and focus on the rest. In one frequently cited experiment, however, this assumption appeared to break down. Researchers set up a tasting stand in a grocery store that offered either six or twenty-four varieties of olive oil. Although the larger display attracted more visitors, shoppers who saw only six varieties were far more likely to buy a bottle. Many of those who stopped at the larger display tasted several oils, hesitated, and walked away empty-handed. The researchers concluded that an abundance of options can ( 1 ).

The idea, which became known as "choice overload," quickly spread beyond the university. Business consultants advised companies to trim their product lines, and some employers reduced the number of investment funds offered in their retirement-savings plans. Popular books on decision-making cited the study as evidence that modern consumers were suffering from too much freedom. ( 2 ), the phenomenon proved surprisingly difficult to reproduce. When other research teams repeated similar experiments with products ranging from chocolates to music downloads, many found that larger assortments had little or no negative effect on purchases. One review that combined the results of dozens of studies concluded that, on average, the effect was close to zero.

This does not mean that choice overload is simply a myth. Rather, many researchers now believe that it appears only under particular conditions. People are most likely to feel overwhelmed when the options are difficult to compare, when they are under time pressure, or when they ( 3 ). A wine expert choosing from a list of fifty bottles, for example, can quickly narrow down the possibilities by region and grape, whereas a beginner may find the same list bewildering and leave without ordering anything at all. The key question, then, may not be how many options people are given, but whether they have the knowledge and tools to make sense of them. Stores and websites that help customers sort and filter products may therefore be able to offer wide selections without driving buyers away.

choices: make shoppers more willing to spend
improve the quality of the products sold
encourage stores to lower their prices
paralyze rather than empower decision-makers
questions.why: 品数が多いと人は集まるが、買う人は少ない、という実験結果のまとめ。選択肢の多さが決断を妨げる（paralyze）。もっとお金を使う・品質が上がる・値下げは実験の内容と関係ない。

choices: Under closer scrutiny, however
As a result of this popularity
In much the same way
For precisely this reason
questions.why: 前は「考えが広まった」、後ろは「再現が難しかった・効果はほぼゼロ」。逆の流れなので however を含む「よく調べると、しかし」。As a result・In much the same way・For precisely this reason は順接で合わない。

choices: have already made similar purchases
are shopping with experienced friends
lack a clear sense of what they prefer
know the products extremely well
questions.why: 直後の例で、専門家はすぐ絞れるが初心者は戸惑う、とある。だから「何が好みか分かっていない時」に圧倒される。know the products extremely well は専門家側で逆。他の2つは本文に根拠が無い。

sets.passage:
Keeping Time on the Rails

Until the middle of the nineteenth century, most towns set their clocks according to local solar time, declaring it noon when the sun reached its highest point in the sky. Because the sun's position changes as one travels east or west, towns only a short distance apart often kept slightly different times. A town fifty miles to the west of another might be several minutes behind it. In most communities, a clock on the town hall served as the official reference, and residents adjusted their pocket watches to match it. For centuries, ( 1 ). Few people traveled far in a single day, and a journey by horse-drawn coach was so slow that a difference of a few minutes hardly mattered.

The arrival of the railways changed this situation dramatically. Trains could cover in an hour a distance that had once taken a full day, and passengers relied on printed timetables to plan their journeys. At first, each railway company simply used the time kept at its own headquarters, so a single station might display several clocks showing different times for different lines. Travelers who misread a timetable could easily miss a connection, and the risk of collisions on shared tracks made accurate timekeeping a matter of safety as well as convenience. Railway companies ( 2 ), dividing the land into broad zones in which every clock showed the same hour.

The change was not welcomed by everyone. Some critics complained that time belonged to the sun, not to businesses, and argued that ordinary people should not have to adjust their lives to suit train schedules. A number of towns stubbornly continued to keep their own local time for years, and some public clocks were even fitted with two minute hands, one for local time and one for railway time. Over the following decades, however, standard time was ( 3 ). Schools, banks, and post offices gradually followed the railways' lead, and the second minute hand disappeared from public clocks. Today, most people would be surprised to learn that the hour on their watch was once a matter of local custom rather than a fixed, shared agreement.

choices: travelers complained constantly about the confusion
these discrepancies caused few practical problems
towns competed to keep the most accurate time
clocks were regarded as too expensive to own
questions.why: 直後に「1日に遠くへ行く人は少なく、馬車は遅いので数分の差は問題にならなかった」とある。だから時刻のずれは困らなかった。constantly complained は逆。正確さの競争・時計の値段は本文に無い。

choices: eventually agreed to adopt a common time
decided to stop publishing timetables
began building separate tracks for each line
allowed passengers to set their own schedules
questions.why: 後ろの「地域を大きな帯に分け、その中の時計はすべて同じ時刻」から、共通の時刻を採用したと分かる。時刻表をやめる・路線ごとの線路・乗客が決める、は混乱の解決にならない。

choices: woven so deeply into daily life that few questioned it
abandoned in favor of the older system
used only by the railway companies themselves
considered a threat to public safety
questions.why: However で反対派の話から転じ、「今では昔は地域ごとだったと知ると驚く」と続く。だから標準時が生活に深く根付いた。旧制度に戻った・鉄道だけが使った・安全への脅威、は最後の文と矛盾する。

sets.passage:
The Return of the Beaver

In many parts of Europe, beavers were hunted almost to extinction for their fur and meat, and by the early twentieth century only a few small populations remained. In recent decades, however, conservation groups have reintroduced the animals to rivers where they had been absent for hundreds of years. Ecologists often describe beavers as "ecosystem engineers" because few other creatures reshape their surroundings so thoroughly. Their sharp front teeth, which never stop growing, allow them to cut through trunks far thicker than their own bodies. By felling trees and building dams from branches and mud, a single family of beavers can transform a narrow stream into a series of ponds and marshes.

These changes ( 1 ). The still water behind a dam provides breeding grounds for frogs and insects, which in turn attract birds and bats. Fallen trees create open, sunny areas where new plants can take root, and the dead wood offers shelter for beetles and fungi. Researchers have also found that beaver ponds store water during dry periods and slow the movement of water after heavy rain, releasing it gradually rather than all at once. In some places, streams that once dried up every summer now flow throughout the year.

Not everyone, however, is pleased to see beavers return. Farmers have complained that dams cause water to spread onto their fields, damaging crops and making the ground too soft for machinery. Landowners have also lost valuable trees, and blocked drainage pipes can cost a great deal to repair. Some residents also worry that the animals may wander into towns and block the channels that carry water under roads. ( 2 ), several regions have introduced programs that pay for devices that control water levels behind dams, as well as compensation for landowners whose property is damaged. In extreme cases, wildlife officers are permitted to move a beaver family to a more suitable location. Supporters of reintroduction admit that these measures require time and money, but they argue that the ecological benefits far outweigh the costs. As one ecologist put it, the long-term success of the project may depend less on the beavers themselves than on ( 3 ).

choices: mostly harm the fish living downstream
make the rivers too cold for wildlife
benefit a wide range of other species

sets.passage:
Learning Through Productive Failure

In a typical mathematics classroom, lessons follow a familiar pattern. The teacher first demonstrates a method, works through several examples, and then asks students to practice similar problems on their own. This approach is efficient, and it allows students to experience success quickly. In recent years, however, a number of education researchers have argued that it may be reversing the most effective order of learning. They advocate an approach known as "productive failure," in which students are given challenging, unfamiliar problems before receiving any instruction on how to solve them. Proponents argue that this initial struggle, far from being wasted time, prepares the mind to learn. Predictably, most students fail to find the correct solution. Only afterward does the teacher explain the standard method, often by comparing it with the students' own attempts.

Supporters point to a study conducted at the Westbrook Institute of Education, in which two groups of thirteen-year-olds were taught how to measure the spread of a set of data. One group received a conventional lesson followed by practice, while the other spent the first half of the lesson struggling to invent its own measures. When both groups were tested a week later, their performance on routine calculation questions was almost identical. On questions that required students to explain why a formula worked, or to apply it to an unfamiliar situation, however, the group that had struggled first scored considerably higher. The researchers suggested that generating several flawed solutions had forced students to draw on what they already knew and made them aware of the gaps in their understanding. As a result, when the correct method was finally presented, they could appreciate what problem it solved rather than simply memorizing its steps.

Critics caution that the benefits of struggle are far from guaranteed. For failure to be productive, the initial problem must be carefully designed: difficult enough to require genuine thought, yet accessible enough that students can make several reasonable attempts. Students who lack basic background knowledge may be unable to generate any meaningful ideas at all, and for them, a long period of confusion can lead to frustration and a loss of confidence rather than deeper understanding. Teachers, too, report that the approach is demanding. They must resist the urge to rescue struggling students, manage the anxiety that some students feel when they cannot find an answer, and explain to parents why lessons seem to involve so much getting things wrong. Lessons built around initial failure also take longer to plan and to teach, which can be a serious drawback in schools where teachers must cover a crowded curriculum before national examinations.

Most researchers therefore recommend using productive failure selectively. Rather than replacing conventional instruction altogether, it may be most valuable when introducing a small number of core concepts that students will build on for years. Some researchers also recommend that teachers openly discuss with students why the struggle is part of the plan, so that failure is seen as a normal step rather than a personal shortcoming. Used in this way, a carefully planned failure may turn out to be one of the most useful experiences a student can have.

questions.q: What distinguishes the "productive failure" approach from conventional mathematics instruction?
choices: Students practice a large number of similar problems until they can solve them without errors.
Teachers deliberately give students incorrect methods so that they learn to spot mistakes.
Students are asked to work on problems before they have been taught a method for solving them.
Students are allowed to choose which problems they want to work on during the lesson.
questions.why: 第1段落：指導を受ける前に難しい未知の問題を与え、後で正しい方法を説明する。大量の練習は従来型の方。先生がわざと誤った方法を教える、生徒が問題を選ぶ、は本文に無い。

questions.q: What did the study at the Westbrook Institute of Education suggest?
choices: Struggling first seemed to deepen students' understanding of why a method works, though it did not improve routine calculation.
Students who received a conventional lesson were better at explaining formulas than those who struggled first.
The students who struggled first became faster at performing calculations than the other group.
Both groups performed equally well on every type of question, showing that the order of teaching is unimportant.
questions.why: 第2段落：計算問題はほぼ同じ、説明や応用の問題で先に苦労した組がかなり上。計算が速くなったとは書いていない。従来組が説明で上、すべての問題で同じ、は逆。

questions.q: What is one concern that critics raise about productive failure?
choices: Parents often demand that teachers use the approach in every lesson.
Well-designed problems make the lessons too easy for most students.
Teachers tend to give students the correct answers too late in the year.
Students without sufficient prior knowledge may become discouraged instead of learning more deeply.
questions.why: 第3段落：基礎知識が無い生徒は意味のある案を出せず、混乱が続くと自信を失う。保護者は「なぜ間違えてばかりか」を説明される側で、全授業での使用を求めてはいない。他も本文と合わない。

sets.passage:
The Ocean's Twilight Zone

Between roughly 200 and 1,000 meters below the surface of the ocean lies a region that scientists call the mesopelagic zone, or, more evocatively, the "twilight zone." Sunlight here is too faint to support plant growth, yet the zone is home to an astonishing variety of animals, from tiny shrimp-like crustaceans to fish no longer than a finger that produce their own light. Because it is so difficult and expensive to study, the twilight zone remains one of the least understood environments on the planet. Most of what is known about it comes from brief expeditions using specialized nets, cameras, and underwater robots.

One of its most remarkable features is a daily movement of animals that some researchers describe as the largest migration on Earth. Each evening, enormous numbers of fish and other creatures rise toward the surface to feed on plankton under the cover of darkness. Before dawn, they descend again to the dim depths, where they are less visible to predators. Some animals travel several hundred meters each way, a journey comparable to a person walking many kilometers twice a day. This journey has consequences far beyond the animals themselves. Plankton near the surface absorb carbon from the atmosphere, and when migrating animals eat them and then release waste or die at depth, much of that carbon is carried down into the deep ocean, where it can remain for centuries. The twilight zone, in other words, plays a significant role in regulating the planet's climate.

For many years, scientists believed that the total mass of fish in the zone was relatively modest. These estimates were based largely on catches made with research nets. More recently, however, surveys using sound waves to detect fish have produced figures many times higher. Researchers now suspect that the earlier surveys greatly underestimated the population, partly because many twilight zone fish are able to sense approaching nets and swim away from them. Other species are so fragile that they are torn apart inside the nets, leaving little trace in the catch.

These new estimates have attracted the attention of the fishing industry. Twilight zone fish are generally too small and oily to be eaten by people, but they could be ground into fishmeal and oil for use in fish farming, an industry that has grown rapidly as demand for seafood has risen. Supporters argue that this vast, untouched resource could reduce pressure on overfished species closer to the surface. Several countries have already shown interest in issuing licenses for experimental fishing. Many marine scientists, however, urge caution. They point out that so little is known about the zone's food webs that it is impossible to predict how large-scale fishing would affect them. If the number of migrating animals fell sharply, less carbon might be transported to the deep ocean, and the consequences for the climate could be serious. Moreover, many larger animals, such as tuna and whales, depend on twilight zone species for food. For now, the scientists argue, the priority should be to understand this hidden world before deciding whether it can safely be exploited.

questions.q: What does the author say about the daily movement of animals in the twilight zone?
choices: It occurs mainly because the animals are searching for warmer water at night.
It has become less common as predators near the surface have increased.
It helps transfer carbon from the surface of the ocean to much greater depths.
It is the main reason that plants are unable to grow in the zone.
questions.why: 第2段落：表層でプランクトンを食べ、深い所で排せつ・死ぬことで炭素が深海に運ばれる。夜に上がるのは暖かい水ではなくエサのため。捕食者の増加・植物が育たない原因、は本文に無い。

questions.q: Why have estimates of the number of fish in the twilight zone changed?
choices: Fishing companies have recently released their own data on catches in the zone.
New survey methods revealed that net-based studies had probably missed many fish.
The fish population has grown because fewer predators now live in the zone.
Researchers discovered that fish from the surface were moving into deeper water.
questions.why: 第3段落：音波を使った調査で何倍もの数字が出た。網に近づくと逃げる魚が多く、網の調査は少なく見積もっていた。漁業会社のデータ・天敵の減少・表層の魚の移動は書かれていない。

questions.q: What is the main concern of the marine scientists mentioned in the final paragraph?
choices: Large-scale fishing could disrupt important natural processes before they are properly understood.
Fishmeal made from twilight zone fish would be unsafe for use in fish farming.
The fishing industry lacks the technology needed to catch fish at such depths.
Demand for seafood will soon fall, making the new fishery unprofitable.
questions.why: 最終段落：食物網がほとんど分かっていないので影響が予測できず、炭素の運搬やマグロ・クジラのエサに響くおそれ。まず理解を、という主張。魚粉の安全性・技術不足・需要の減少は述べられていない。

sets.passage:
Designing Cities for the Ear

For most of the twentieth century, city planners treated sound as a form of pollution. Noise from traffic, construction, and industry was measured in decibels, and the goal of policy was simple: reduce the numbers. Laws limited how loud machines could be, and walls were built along highways to block the roar of passing vehicles. These measures brought real benefits, since long-term exposure to loud noise has been linked to sleep problems and stress. In many cities, maps were produced showing which streets exceeded legal limits, and money was spent on quieter engines and road surfaces.

In recent decades, however, a growing number of researchers have argued that decibel readings tell only part of the story. Advocates of what is known as the "soundscape" approach point out that people do not experience sound simply as volume. The splash of a fountain or the chatter of a busy market can be just as loud as nearby traffic, yet most people find such sounds pleasant or even calming. What matters, these researchers argue, is how people perceive and interpret the sounds around them, and that perception depends heavily on context, expectations, and the meaning people attach to a sound. A dog barking in the distance may go unnoticed in a farming village but feel intrusive in a quiet apartment late at night.

One often-cited example is the redesign of Marlow Square, a busy public space in a mid-sized city. Rather than attempting to block the noise of the surrounding roads, designers added a series of fountains, planted trees to attract birds, and arranged seating so that visitors faced away from the traffic. Measurements taken after the project showed that overall sound levels in the square had barely changed. Yet in surveys, residents described the area as far more relaxing than before, and the number of people who used the square during their lunch breaks more than doubled. Visitors also reported that they were less aware of the traffic, even though it was still clearly audible. For supporters, the results showed that cities can improve people's experience of sound without the enormous expense of eliminating noise at its source.

Not everyone is convinced. Some public health experts warn that pleasant sounds may merely mask harmful noise rather than reduce it, and that the body may continue to react to traffic noise even when the mind no longer notices it. Others worry that the soundscape approach could provide officials with an attractive excuse to avoid more costly measures, such as rerouting heavy vehicles or installing quieter road surfaces. Neighborhoods located beside busy highways, they argue, need genuine reductions in noise, not decorative fountains.

Most researchers in the field see the two approaches as complementary rather than competing. Reducing harmful noise remains essential, but once the worst problems have been addressed, thoughtful design can help turn a merely tolerable environment into one that people actively enjoy. Several cities have begun to involve residents in "sound walks," in which participants note which sounds they value and which they would like to see removed.

questions.q: How does the soundscape approach differ from traditional noise control?
choices: It aims to eliminate all sounds from public spaces in cities.
It focuses on how people perceive sounds rather than only on how loud they are.
It relies on stricter laws that limit the volume of machines.
It measures noise more accurately than earlier decibel readings.
questions.why: 第2段落：音を音量だけで捉えず、人がどう受け取り解釈するかが大事、とする。すべての音をなくす・法律での規制は従来型の側。測定の正確さの話ではない。

questions.q: What was the result of the Marlow Square project?
choices: Residents found the square more pleasant even though sound levels hardly changed.
Sound levels in the square fell sharply after the fountains were added.
Fewer people used the square because the fountains were too noisy.
The project cost more than eliminating the traffic noise would have.
questions.why: 第3段落：全体の音の大きさはほとんど変わらないのに、住民はずっとくつろげると答え、昼休みの利用者は2倍以上。音量が大きく下がった・利用者が減った、は逆。費用の比較は書かれていない。

questions.q: Why are some critics cautious about the soundscape approach?
choices: They believe fountains and trees are too costly for most cities to maintain.
They think residents near highways prefer the sound of traffic to fountains.
They argue that birdsong can cause stress when it is heard for long periods.
They fear it may be used to avoid the more expensive work of reducing harmful noise.
questions.why: 第4段落：心地よい音は有害な騒音を隠すだけかもしれず、交通の迂回や静かな舗装など費用のかかる対策を避ける口実になりうる、と心配している。維持費・住民の好み・鳥の声のストレスは本文に無い。

sets.passage:
Do Trees Talk to Each Other?

Over the past three decades, few ideas in ecology have captured the public imagination as powerfully as the "wood wide web." According to this idea, the trees in a forest are linked underground by vast networks of fungi that grow around and into their roots. These fungi, known as mycorrhizal fungi, are said to act like a living internet, allowing trees to share sugars, water, and even chemical warning signals with one another. In the most popular versions of the story, large, old "mother trees" use the networks to feed their own seedlings growing in the shade, and dying trees pass their remaining resources on to their neighbors. Some versions even suggest that trees can recognize their relatives and send them a larger share of resources than they send to unrelated neighbors. The forest, in this view, is less a collection of competing individuals than a cooperative community.

It is not difficult to see why the idea became so popular. It appeared in best-selling books, award-winning documentaries, and even feature films, and it offered a moving picture of nature that seemed to challenge the image of the forest as a place of ruthless competition for light and nutrients. For many readers, the notion that trees nurture their young and support their sick neighbors was not only fascinating but also deeply comforting. Some foresters and conservation groups began citing the networks as a reason to protect old trees, arguing that cutting them down would destroy the hubs on which the whole forest depended.

In recent years, however, a number of scientists have begun to question whether the evidence supports such dramatic claims. One team of researchers carefully reviewed several dozen field studies that had been cited in support of the wood wide web. Their conclusions were striking. First, they found that there was surprisingly little direct evidence that fungal networks connecting many trees are common in real forests. Proving that two trees are linked by the same fungus is technically difficult, and only a handful of studies had attempted to do so, most of them in a small number of forest types. Moreover, the fungal species involved can change over time, so a link observed in one season may not exist in the next. Second, although some experiments had shown that carbon could move from one tree to another, it was often unclear whether it had traveled through the fungal network or by some other route, such as through the soil. And even where transfer did occur, the amounts were usually too small to make a meaningful difference to the receiving tree.

The third finding concerned the claim that networks help seedlings survive. When the reviewers examined experiments that tested this idea, they found that the results were remarkably inconsistent. In some studies, seedlings connected to older trees grew better; in others, they grew worse; and in many, there was no noticeable difference at all. The reviewers argued that the positive results had been widely publicized, while the negative or neutral ones had been largely overlooked.

This last point raised a broader concern about how scientific ideas spread. The reviewers analyzed how often the original studies had been cited in later research papers, and they discovered a clear pattern. Studies that appeared to support the wood wide web were cited far more often than those that did not, and when they were cited, their findings were frequently described in stronger terms than the original authors had used. A cautious statement that carbon "may" move between trees under certain laboratory conditions, for example, might become a confident claim that trees "share" food in nature. Over time, the reviewers suggested, these small exaggerations accumulated until the public story bore only a loose resemblance to the underlying evidence.

Not all scientists accept this critique. Some researchers who helped develop the idea argue that the reviewers set an unreasonably high standard of proof, and that the overall pattern of evidence, though incomplete, still points toward meaningful connections between trees. They also note that forests are enormously complex, and that the absence of evidence in a few studies does not prove that networks are unimportant. They also point out that seedlings planted in sterilized soil, without access to fungi, often struggle to survive. Both sides, however, agree on several basic points: mycorrhizal fungi are essential to the health of most trees, they exchange nutrients with their host plants, and far more research under natural conditions is needed.

The debate also has practical implications. If the strongest claims about mother trees turn out to be exaggerated, does that mean old trees are less valuable than conservationists have argued? Not necessarily. Large, old trees store huge amounts of carbon, provide habitats for countless species, and influence the conditions in which younger trees grow, regardless of whether they feed them through fungal networks. The lesson of the controversy, some ecologists suggest, is not that the forest is a simple battleground after all, but that policies are on firmer ground when they rest on what has actually been demonstrated rather than on the most appealing version of a story. Some researchers add that the episode should encourage scientists and journalists alike to use more modest language when describing new findings to the public.

questions.q: What made the idea of the "wood wide web" so appealing to the general public?
choices: It proved that trees compete fiercely with one another for light and nutrients.
It was based on a large number of studies conducted in many types of forest.
It suggested that old trees could be cut down without harming the forest.
It portrayed forests as caring communities, a picture many people found emotionally moving.
questions.why: 第2段落：木が子を育て弱った仲間を支える、という像が魅力的で心を慰めるものだった。競争の場というイメージを覆したので、激しい競争を証明したは逆。研究が多かった、は第3段落で否定。老木を切ってよい、も逆。

questions.q: According to the review described in the passage, what was one problem with the evidence for carbon transfer between trees?
choices: The amounts of carbon transferred were usually large enough to harm the receiving tree.
Researchers had found that fungi prevent carbon from moving through the soil.
It was often uncertain whether the carbon had passed through fungi or along another path.
Most experiments had been carried out on trees that were already dying.
questions.why: 第3段落：炭素が別の木へ移っても、菌のネットワーク経由か土など別の経路かが分からないことが多かった。量は「意味のある差を生むには少なすぎた」ので、害を与えるほど多いは逆。他の2つは本文に無い。

questions.q: What did the reviewers discover when they examined how the original studies had been cited?
choices: Studies that did not support the idea were usually cited first in later papers.
Supportive findings were cited more often and were often described more confidently than their authors intended.
Most researchers had refused to cite studies about mycorrhizal fungi at all.
The original authors had made stronger claims than later researchers repeated.
questions.why: 第5段落：支持する研究ほど多く引用され、しかも元の著者より強い言い方で紹介された（may → share）。支持しない研究が先に引用された、元の著者の方が強く言った、は逆。

questions.q: Which of the following statements would the author of the passage most likely agree with?
choices: Even if some claims about tree networks were exaggerated, there are still good reasons to protect old trees.
The debate has shown that mycorrhizal fungi play no important role in forest health.
Scientists who developed the wood wide web idea have now abandoned it completely.
Forest policy should be based on whichever version of a scientific story is most popular.
questions.why: 最終段落：老木は炭素を蓄え多くの生き物のすみかになるので、ネットワーク説が誇張でも価値は残る。菌は健康に不可欠と両者が同意しているので「役割なし」は誤り。提唱者は反論しているので放棄していない。最後の文は「魅力的な話より実証されたことに基づく方がよい」なので4つ目は逆。

sets.passage:
Bringing a Language Back

On the small, windswept island of Varn, lying some forty kilometers off the northern coast of the mainland, a language called Ostrani was once spoken in nearly every home. For centuries, islanders used it to bargain at the harbor, to sing at weddings, and to name the hundreds of rocks, currents, and fishing grounds that surrounded their coast. By the end of the twentieth century, however, fewer than three hundred fluent speakers remained, almost all of them over the age of sixty. Linguists who visited the island predicted that within a generation Ostrani would disappear entirely.

The decline had not been caused by any single event. As the island's fishing industry shrank from the 1950s onward, many young people moved to the mainland in search of work, and the national language became essential for anyone hoping to find a job or continue their education. Schools on the island taught exclusively in the national language, and teachers often advised parents that speaking Ostrani at home would only confuse their children. Many parents, wanting the best possible future for their sons and daughters, took this advice. They continued to speak Ostrani with their own parents and neighbors but switched to the national language when addressing their children. Within a single generation, the chain of transmission from parent to child had been broken. The children grew up understanding some Ostrani but rarely speaking it, and their own children grew up knowing almost none. Over time, the language also came to be associated with poverty and an old-fashioned way of life, which made some young islanders reluctant to use it even when they could.

The turning point came in the 1990s, when a group of islanders, many of them the children of those who had stopped speaking the language at home, formed an association to revive it. They began by recording elderly speakers telling stories and describing traditional crafts, creating an archive of several thousand hours of conversation. Volunteers transcribed the recordings and added translations, so that learners could study them at home. Their most ambitious project, however, was a "language nest," a preschool in which children between the ages of two and five spent their days with older speakers who used nothing but Ostrani. The idea was based on the observation that young children acquire languages most easily through everyday interaction rather than formal lessons. At first, only six families enrolled their children. Today, the nest has a waiting list, and its graduates can continue their education in Ostrani at a primary school that teaches most subjects in the language.

For adults, the association developed a different approach. In its "master and apprentice" program, a fluent elder and a younger learner commit to spending at least ten hours a week together, cooking, fishing, or repairing nets while speaking only Ostrani. Participants say the program has benefits that go beyond language. Elders who had once felt that their knowledge was worthless report a renewed sense of purpose, and learners describe forming relationships with people they might otherwise never have met. The program has also produced practical knowledge: several apprentices have compiled dictionaries of fishing terms and place names that had never been written down.

The revival has not been free of tension, however. Because Ostrani had never had a standard written form, the association needed to create one in order to produce textbooks and teaching materials. In doing so, it chose spellings and grammatical forms based mainly on the variety spoken in the island's largest village. Elders from other parts of the island sometimes complain that the young people who learn from these textbooks speak a version of the language that sounds artificial to them, and a few have refused to take part in the program altogether. Others have proposed allowing several spellings to coexist, though teachers say this would make materials far harder to prepare. Some young learners, for their part, feel discouraged when older speakers correct them constantly or tell them that their Ostrani "is not the real thing." Linguists who study language revival say that such disagreements are common, and that the emergence of "new speakers" whose language differs from that of earlier generations is a natural part of the process rather than a sign of failure.

Measuring the success of the revival is not straightforward. According to the association's most recent survey, around nine hundred people on the island can now hold a conversation in Ostrani, triple the number of thirty years ago. Yet most of them use the language mainly at school, at association events, or online, and only a few dozen families speak it as their main language at home. Some supporters worry that Ostrani is becoming a language that people study rather than one they live in. The association has responded by organizing weekly gatherings in cafés and at the harbor, where speakers of all ages are encouraged to use the language informally. Others are more optimistic. They point out that the first generation of language-nest graduates is now beginning to have children of its own, and that several of these young parents have chosen to raise their children in Ostrani. If that trend continues, the chain that was broken half a century ago may finally be restored.

questions.q: Why did the number of children speaking Ostrani decline?
choices: Many parents spoke the national language to their children because they thought it would give them better opportunities.
The government passed a law that banned the use of Ostrani on the island.
Elderly speakers refused to teach the language to people outside their families.
Children found Ostrani too difficult to learn because it had no written form.

In laboratories around the world, scientists are now able to grow real animal meat without raising and slaughtering animals. The process begins with a small sample of cells taken from a living animal. These cells are placed in large steel tanks filled with a nutrient-rich liquid, where they multiply until they form tissue that can be shaped into products such as burgers or chicken nuggets. Several start-up companies have already offered cultivated meat to diners in a small number of restaurants, and investors have poured large sums of money into the industry.

Supporters believe that cultivated meat could solve several problems at once. Conventional livestock farming requires vast areas of land for grazing and for growing animal feed, and it is responsible for a significant share of the world's greenhouse gas emissions. Producing meat in tanks, they argue, could dramatically reduce the land and water needed to feed a growing global population. In addition, animal welfare groups point out that the technology would allow people to continue eating meat without causing animals to suffer.

Skeptics, however, question whether these promises can be fulfilled. At present, producing cultivated meat is extremely expensive, partly because the nutrient liquid in which the cells grow is costly to make. Scaling up production to the level of an industrial meat plant would require enormous investments in equipment and energy, and some researchers have calculated that, if that energy comes from fossil fuels, the environmental benefits could be much smaller than advertised. There are also doubts about whether consumers will accept the product. In surveys, many people say they find the idea of meat grown in a factory unnatural or even disturbing.

Farmers' organizations have raised further concerns. They worry that if cultivated meat becomes popular, rural communities that depend on livestock farming could lose their main source of income, and traditional knowledge about raising animals could disappear. Some have called for strict labeling rules so that consumers can clearly distinguish between conventional and cultivated products. Whether the technology becomes a common part of people's diets or remains a costly curiosity may depend as much on public attitudes and government regulation as on scientific progress.

A growing number of companies now use computer software to help them decide which job applicants to interview. These programs scan résumés for relevant skills and experience, and some go further, analyzing applicants' answers to online questionnaires or even their facial expressions and tone of voice in recorded video interviews. For employers that receive thousands of applications for a single position, such tools promise to make the hiring process far faster and cheaper.

Advocates argue that automated screening can also make hiring fairer. Human recruiters, they point out, are influenced by unconscious biases. They may favor applicants who attended the same university as themselves or who have names that sound familiar, and they may judge candidates differently depending on how tired they are at the end of the day. A well-designed program, by contrast, applies the same criteria to every applicant. Some companies that have adopted such tools report that they now interview a more diverse range of candidates than before.

Critics, however, warn that automated systems can reproduce and even magnify the very biases they are supposed to remove. Many programs learn what a "good" employee looks like by studying data about a company's past hires. If those hires were mostly drawn from a narrow group, the software may learn to rank similar applicants more highly and quietly screen out others. Because the programs' decision-making processes are often complex and kept secret by the companies that sell them, it can be extremely difficult for rejected applicants to find out why they were turned down, or to challenge the decision.

There are also concerns about the methods used in some systems. Experts in psychology have questioned whether facial expressions or speech patterns recorded during a short video can reveal anything meaningful about a person's ability to do a job. In response to such criticism, some governments have begun to consider rules that would require employers to inform applicants when software is used, and to have the systems tested regularly for unfair outcomes. Others argue that the final decision on whom to hire should always be made by a human being.

Many large cities have long struggled with heavy traffic in their central districts. Traffic jams waste time, raise transportation costs for businesses, and contribute to air pollution. In an attempt to address these problems, a number of cities have introduced what are known as congestion charges. Under such schemes, drivers must pay a fee to enter the city center during busy hours, with cameras recording the license plates of vehicles that cross the boundary. Drivers who fail to pay within a set period receive a fine, while residents of the zone and some essential vehicles may be given discounts.

Supporters say the results have been impressive. In cities that have adopted congestion charges, the number of vehicles entering the center has often fallen significantly within the first year, and travel times for buses and delivery vehicles have improved. Air quality in central streets has also tended to get better. Moreover, the money raised by the charges is frequently used to improve public transportation, for instance by adding bus routes or extending train services, which gives residents more alternatives to driving.

Nevertheless, congestion charges remain controversial. Opponents argue that the fees fall most heavily on people with lower incomes, who may have no choice but to drive into the city for work, especially if they work at night when public transportation is limited. Wealthier drivers, on the other hand, can simply pay the charge and enjoy emptier roads. Some small business owners in charging zones have also complained that customers now prefer to shop at suburban malls with free parking, leading to a drop in sales, though others say that quieter streets have made their areas more attractive to shoppers on foot.

In addition, critics note that the benefits of the schemes depend heavily on local conditions. In cities without good public transportation, a congestion charge may simply push traffic onto the roads just outside the charging zone, creating new jams in residential neighborhoods. For this reason, many urban planners argue that a charge should be introduced only as part of a wider strategy that includes investment in public transportation and safe routes for cyclists and pedestrians. Without such measures, they warn, a congestion charge may be seen by residents as little more than an unfair tax.

For generations, a university degree has been regarded as the most reliable route to a well-paid professional career. In recent years, however, a growing number of people have been turning to so-called "micro-credentials." These are short courses, often offered online by universities, technology companies, or professional associations, that certify a person's skills in a specific area, such as data analysis or project management. Many can be completed in a few weeks or months and cost only a fraction of a traditional degree.

Supporters argue that micro-credentials are well suited to a rapidly changing job market. As new technologies transform industries, workers increasingly need to update their skills throughout their careers rather than relying on what they learned in their early twenties. Short, focused courses allow them to do so without leaving their jobs. Supporters also point out that micro-credentials can open doors for people who cannot afford the time or money required for a full degree, such as working parents or those living far from a university. Employers, too, can use them to train staff quickly in the specific skills they need.

However, critics have raised questions about the value of these qualifications. Because they are offered by so many different organizations, their quality varies enormously, and employers may find it hard to judge what a particular certificate actually represents. Some surveys suggest that, although employers say they value specific skills, many still prefer to hire applicants with traditional degrees. There is a risk, critics say, that workers will spend money on a series of short courses that do little to improve their job prospects.

Educators have expressed another concern. A university education, they argue, is not only about acquiring job-related skills. It also aims to develop critical thinking, communication, and the ability to understand complex problems from different perspectives, abilities that are difficult to teach in a short online course. Some universities are now trying to combine the two approaches by allowing students to build up micro-credentials that can later be counted toward a full degree. Whether this model becomes widespread may depend on how much trust employers and students come to place in these new forms of certification.

Only a decade ago, analyzing a person's genes was an expensive procedure carried out mainly in hospitals and research laboratories. Today, anyone can order a genetic testing kit online for a modest price. After sending a small sample of saliva to the company, customers receive a report that may describe their ancestry, their likelihood of developing certain medical conditions, and even traits such as how their bodies respond to caffeine. Millions of people around the world have now used these services.

Many customers find the results valuable. Learning that they have an increased risk of a particular disease can motivate people to change their diet, exercise more, or arrange regular medical checkups, potentially allowing problems to be detected at an early stage. For others, information about their family origins has led to a deeper understanding of their identity, and in some cases, people have even discovered relatives they never knew existed.

Medical experts, however, caution that such tests can be misleading. Most common diseases are influenced by many genes as well as by lifestyle and environment, so a report stating that a person has a "slightly elevated risk" may be of little practical use. Some customers who receive worrying results experience considerable anxiety, while others who receive reassuring results may wrongly conclude that they do not need to take care of their health. Unlike tests ordered by doctors, these kits are usually not accompanied by professional advice to help people interpret what they mean, and few companies explain the limits of their predictions in a way that ordinary customers can easily understand.

Privacy is another major concern. Genetic data reveals information not only about the person who provided the sample, but also about their parents, children, and other relatives, none of whom agreed to the test. Companies may share data with research partners, and critics worry that it could one day be used by insurers or employers. Although some companies promise to protect their customers' information, the rules governing how genetic data can be stored and shared differ widely between countries. Many experts are therefore calling for clearer regulations before the technology becomes even more widespread.

In recent years, the number of international tourists has grown rapidly, driven by cheaper flights and the spread of online booking services. While tourism brings money and jobs to many communities, some popular destinations have begun to feel overwhelmed. Historic town centers are crowded with visitors, rents have risen as apartments are converted into short-term rentals, and residents complain about noise and litter. In response, a number of cities and regions have introduced special taxes that visitors must pay, often added to the cost of a hotel room or charged as a daily entrance fee.

Supporters argue that such taxes are a fair way to share the costs of tourism. Large numbers of visitors place heavy demands on public services, such as waste collection, public transportation, and the maintenance of historic sites, and it seems reasonable that tourists, rather than local taxpayers alone, should help pay for them. The revenue can also be used to protect the environment or to support affordable housing for residents. Some supporters also hope that higher costs will discourage short day trips, which bring crowds but relatively little income, and encourage visitors to stay longer and spend more money at local businesses.

Critics, however, doubt that such taxes are effective. In many cases, the fees are too small to change visitors' behavior, and popular destinations remain just as crowded as before. If the fees are raised high enough to make a difference, on the other hand, tourism could become a privilege available only to the wealthy. Business owners in the tourism industry also worry that visitors will choose cheaper destinations instead, leading to lost income and jobs.

There are also questions about how the money is spent. In some places, residents complain that tourist tax revenue disappears into general government budgets rather than being used to address the problems caused by tourism. Experts suggest that taxes are most likely to win public support when the authorities clearly explain how the money will be used and when they are combined with other measures, such as limits on short-term rentals or systems that require visitors to book entry to popular sites in advance.
