M: Oh no. That's every presenter's nightmare. What did you do?
W: I tried to talk them through the figures from memory, but I could see their eyes glazing over. The chairman eventually suggested we pick it up next week.
M: Well, at least they didn't reject the proposal outright. That's something, isn't it?
W: That's true. And to be honest, a few of them asked questions I hadn't anticipated, so the extra time will let me strengthen those sections.
Question: What does the woman imply?

questions.q: What does the woman imply?
choices: The board rejected her proposal.
She had not prepared for the presentation.
The delay may turn out to be beneficial.
The chairman criticized her financial figures.
questions.why: 最後に「予想外の質問が出たので、時間ができて補強できる」と言い、延期を前向きにとらえている。却下はされていない（didn't reject outright）。12回も練習した。会長は数字を批判していない。

sets.script:
W: So, have you made up your mind about the car?
M: I'm leaning toward the electric one. The running costs are so much lower, and there's a government rebate this year.
W: But you drive to your parents' place in the mountains almost every weekend. Are there even charging stations out there?
M: There's one in the town nearest to them, but it's often out of order, from what I've read.
W: Then you might end up stranded. What about the hybrid? You'd still save on fuel, and you wouldn't have to worry about finding a charger.
M: You've got a point. I'll take a closer look at the hybrid models before I commit to anything.
Question: Why does the woman have doubts about the electric car?

questions.q: Why does the woman have doubts about the electric car?
choices: It does not qualify for the government rebate.
The man may have trouble charging it on his regular trips.
Its running costs are higher than a hybrid's.
The man's parents dislike electric vehicles.
questions.why: 毎週末山の実家へ行くが、近くの充電所はよく故障している → 立ち往生（stranded）するかも、が女性の心配。補助金はあり、維持費は電気自動車の方が安い。親の好みは出てこない。

sets.script:
M: I heard you got an offer from the Singapore office. Congratulations!
W: Thanks, but I haven't accepted yet. It's a big step up in salary, and the role itself is exactly what I want.
M: So what's holding you back?
W: My husband's job, mainly. His company doesn't have a branch there, and he's just been promoted.
M: Could he work remotely?
W: He asked, but they want him in the office at least three days a week. They did say they might reconsider in a year.
M: Maybe you could ask Singapore to push back your start date.
W: Actually, I'm meeting HR tomorrow to see if they'd let me start next spring. That would give us time to figure things out.
Question: What will the woman do tomorrow?

questions.q: What will the woman do tomorrow?
choices: Ask whether she can begin the new job at a later date.
Accept the offer from the Singapore office.
Ask her husband's company about remote work.
Turn down the position in Singapore.
questions.why: 明日人事と会い、来春から始められるか確かめる。まだ受諾も辞退もしていない。在宅勤務は夫がすでに会社に聞いて断られた。

sets.script:
W: Are you still helping out at the film festival this weekend?
M: I'm supposed to be, but I've run into a scheduling problem. They've put me on the ticket desk Saturday morning, and that's exactly when my cousin's wedding rehearsal is.
W: Oh no. Can't you just tell them you're unavailable? Or swap shifts with another volunteer?
M: I tried. The coordinator says all the other Saturday slots are full, and she's too busy to reorganize the schedule.
W: I'm volunteering on Sunday afternoon. If you can take my shift, I could probably cover yours on Saturday. I'm free that morning.
M: Really? Are you sure you don't mind? That would save me. I'll let the coordinator know right away.
Question: What does the woman offer to do?

questions.q: What does the woman offer to do?
choices: Exchange volunteer shifts with the man.
Attend the wedding rehearsal in his place.
Ask the coordinator to change the schedule.
Work both weekend shifts by herself.
questions.why: 女性の日曜午後の担当を男性が、男性の土曜朝を女性が受け持つ＝交換。調整役は忙しくて組み直せないと言っている。両方を1人で、ではない。

sets.script:
M: Have you had a chance to review the draft labels for the fossil exhibition?
W: I have, and I'm a bit concerned. They're accurate, but they read like extracts from a scientific journal.
M: Well, our curators wrote them. They want to make sure nothing is oversimplified.
W: I understand, but our visitor surveys show most people spend less than ten seconds reading each label. Families with young children make up nearly half our audience.
M: So what do you propose?
W: Keep a short, engaging headline and two or three plain sentences on each label. The detailed information can go on the museum's website, with a code visitors can scan.
M: The curators might push back, but I'll put it to them.
Question: What does the woman want to do?

questions.q: What does the woman want to do?
choices: Ask the curators to write longer labels.
Remove the labels from the exhibition entirely.
Conduct another survey of museum visitors.
Make the labels simpler and move the detailed content online.
questions.why: 見出しと平易な2〜3文に短くし、詳しい情報はウェブサイトへ、という提案。長くする・全部なくす、は逆。調査はすでにある。

sets.script:
W: I've found a lovely cottage by the lake for our anniversary, but it's booked solid in August.
M: What about September? The kids will be back at school, so it might be quieter anyway.
W: That's the problem. If we go in September, we'd need my mother to look after them for the week, and she's having her hip operation then.
M: Ah, right. Could we ask my sister?
W: She's just started a new job. I'd hate to impose on her.
M: Then why don't we bring the kids along in late July? It wouldn't be quite as romantic, but they'd love the lake.
W: I suppose it'd be nice to go as a family. I'll check if there's anything available.
Question: What will the woman probably do next?

questions.q: What will the woman probably do next?
choices: Ask the man's sister to look after the children.
Book the cottage for a week in September.
Cancel their anniversary trip.
See whether the cottage can be booked for late July.
questions.why: 7月下旬に子ども連れで、という案に賛成し、空きを調べると言った。妹は新しい仕事なので頼みたくない。9月は母の手術で無理。旅行はやめない。

sets.script:
M: The investor from Crestline called. They're willing to put in two million, but they want a seat on our board.
W: A seat on the board? That would give them a say in every major decision.
M: I know. On the other hand, without that money we can't hire the engineers we need to launch by autumn.
W: What about the bank loan we discussed?
M: The bank offered only half the amount, and at a high interest rate.
W: Hmm. Let's not rush into anything. Could you ask Crestline whether they'd accept observer status instead? They'd attend meetings but wouldn't have a vote.
M: Worth a try. I'll call them back this afternoon.
Question: What does the woman want the man to do?

questions.q: What does the woman want the man to do?
choices: Accept the investor's offer as it stands.
Apply for a larger loan from the bank.
Propose giving the investor a more limited role.
Delay the launch until next year.
questions.why: 取締役の席の代わりに、議決権の無いオブザーバーでどうか聞いてほしい＝役割を限る提案。そのまま受ける、は慌てるなと言っている。銀行・延期の話はしていない。

sets.script:
W: Kevin, I've just read the complaint from Mrs. Ortega about her delayed order.
M: I know. I dealt with her on the phone yesterday. She was pretty upset, and I can't say I blame her. She'd been waiting nearly three weeks.
W: According to her email, you told her the delay was the warehouse's fault.
M: Well, it was. They shipped the wrong item.
W: That may be true, but blaming another department makes the whole company look disorganized. Next time, apologize, explain what you're doing to fix the problem, and leave the internal details out of it.
M: Understood. I guess I was just trying to show it wasn't my fault. Should I call her again?
W: Yes, and offer her free express shipping on the replacement.
Question: What is the woman's main point?

questions.q: What is the woman's main point?
choices: The warehouse was not responsible for the mistake.
Mrs. Ortega's complaint was unreasonable.
The man should have offered her a full refund.
The man should avoid blaming other departments when dealing with customers.
questions.why: 他部署のせいにすると会社全体がだらしなく見える、謝って対応を説明し内部の事情は言うな、が要点。倉庫のミスは否定していない（That may be true）。提案は返金ではなく速達無料。

sets.script:
M: Have you finished the grant application yet? It's due on Friday.
W: Almost. I'm just struggling with the section on public impact. The reviewers want to know how our research will benefit society, and honestly, it's pretty theoretical.
M: What about the collaboration with the water treatment company? Our models could help them detect contamination faster.
W: That's true, but we haven't signed anything with them yet. I'd hate to promise something we can't deliver.
M: You don't need a contract. A letter from their research director saying they're interested would be enough to show potential applications.
W: Good idea. That would make the section much more concrete. I'll email her today and ask if she can send one by Thursday.
Question: What will the woman do next?

questions.q: What will the woman do next?
choices: Sign a contract with a water treatment company.
Ask for an extension on the grant deadline.
Request a letter of support from a company.
Rewrite the theoretical part of the application.
questions.why: 研究責任者に、関心を示す手紙を木曜までに送ってもらうようメールする。契約は不要と言われた。締め切りの延長や理論部分の書き直しは話に出ない。

sets.script:
W: You look exhausted, Tom.
M: I am. I nearly fell asleep in this morning's meeting. The couple who moved in upstairs have a baby, and it cries for hours every night. I haven't had a decent night's sleep in weeks.
W: That's tough. Have you spoken to them?
M: What could I say? It's not as if they can switch the baby off. They're probably more exhausted than I am.
W: Fair enough. Babies don't exactly come with a volume control. Have you thought about moving your bed to the other room? Or getting a white-noise machine? My sister swears by hers.
M: Actually, the spare room is directly above the lobby, so it's quieter. I'll try sleeping there for a few nights.
Question: What does the man decide to do?

questions.q: What does the man decide to do?
choices: Complain to the couple living upstairs.
Sleep in a different room in his apartment.
Buy a white-noise machine.
Move to a new apartment.
questions.why: 空き部屋はロビーの上で静かなので、数晩そこで寝てみる。上の夫婦に言っても仕方ない、と苦情は否定。ホワイトノイズの機械は女性の提案で、男性は選んでいない。

sets.script:
W: Daniel, I finished reading your manuscript over the weekend. The writing is wonderful.
M: Thank you. I sense a "but" coming.
W: But it's about 40,000 words longer than our usual length for this kind of book. The printing costs alone would make it hard to price competitively.
M: I've already cut so much. I took out nearly a hundred pages last spring, and every chapter that's left feels essential.
W: I'd suggest looking at chapters six through eight. They're fascinating, but they wander away from your central story. They could make an excellent separate essay collection later.
M: I hadn't thought of it that way. Those chapters did start life as separate pieces. Let me reread them with that in mind.
Question: What does the editor suggest?

questions.q: What does the editor suggest?
choices: Removing some chapters that could be published separately later.
Raising the price of the book.
Adding more detail to the central story.
Publishing the manuscript in two volumes.
questions.why: 6〜8章は本筋から外れるので削り、後で別のエッセイ集にできる、という提案。値上げは競争できないので逆。本筋を足す・2巻に分ける、は言っていない。

sets.script:
M: Thanks for showing me around. The garden is beautiful, but I'm worried about the weather. Our reception is in late October.
W: That's a common concern. If it rains, we can move everything into the glass pavilion. It holds up to 150 guests.
M: We're expecting about 180, though.
W: I see. In that case, we could put up a heated marquee on the lawn as a backup. It's an extra charge, but we only set it up if the forecast looks bad two days before.
M: And if it's not needed?
W: Then you'd only pay a small reservation fee, which is about a tenth of the full price.
M: That sounds reasonable. Let's include that in the contract.
Question: What does the man decide to do?

questions.q: What does the man decide to do?
choices: Reduce the number of guests to 150.
Reserve a tent that will be put up only if the weather looks bad.
Hold the reception in the glass pavilion.
Change the date of the reception.
questions.why: marquee＝大きなテント。2日前の予報が悪い時だけ立てる予備のテントを契約に入れる。招待客は約180人でガラスの建物には入らない。日付の変更はしていない。

parts.title: リスニング Part 2 Passages
parts.desc: 約200語の説明文（科学・社会・文化）を聞き、質問2つの答えを4つから選ぶ。放送は1回
parts.tip: 放送前に2問分の選択肢を見て、話題と問われそうな点（理由・研究結果・批判）を予想する。However / Recent studies suggest の後に話の転換が来る。1問目は前半、2問目は後半から出ることが多い。
parts.intro: Listen to each passage and the questions that follow. Then choose the best answer to each question from the four printed choices. The passage will be played only once.

sets.script:
For a long time, psychologists paid little attention to boredom, regarding it as a trivial and purely unpleasant feeling. In recent years, however, researchers have begun to argue that boredom serves an important purpose. According to this view, boredom acts as a signal, telling us that our current activity is no longer meaningful or rewarding and pushing us to look for something better. In this sense, it resembles pain or hunger: uncomfortable, but useful.

Some studies suggest that this push can even encourage creativity. In one experiment, participants first spent fifteen minutes copying numbers from a telephone directory, a deliberately dull task. They were then asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Compared with a group that had skipped the dull task, the bored participants came up with more ideas, and their ideas were judged to be more original.

Researchers caution, however, that boredom is beneficial only when people respond to it constructively. Those who experience boredom frequently and intensely, a condition known as boredom proneness, are more likely to seek quick distractions, such as checking their phones, rather than pursuing more meaningful goals.
Question 1: What do some researchers now believe about boredom?
Question 2: What did the experiment described by the speaker show?

questions.q: What do some researchers now believe about boredom?
choices: It is a trivial emotion with no real function.
It encourages people to look for more rewarding activities.
It is caused mainly by hunger or physical pain.
It makes people less willing to change their goals.
questions.why: boredom acts as a signal … pushing us to look for something better。痛みや空腹は「似ている」例えで、原因ではない。trivial は昔の見方。

questions.q: What did the experiment described by the speaker show?
choices: People who skipped the dull task thought of more original uses.
Copying numbers improved participants' memory for details.
Bored participants refused to complete the second task.
People who had first done a dull task produced more creative ideas.
questions.why: 退屈な作業をした組の方がアイデアが多く、独創的だった。作業を飛ばした組の方が、は逆。記憶力や作業の拒否は話に出ない。

sets.script:
Many structures built by the ancient Romans, including harbor walls that have been battered by seawater for two thousand years, are still standing today. Modern concrete, by contrast, often begins to crack and crumble within a few decades. Scientists have long tried to understand what made the Roman material so durable.

One clue lies in small white lumps of lime that are scattered throughout Roman concrete. For many years, researchers assumed that these lumps were simply a sign of poor-quality materials or careless mixing. Recent studies, however, suggest that they may have been essential to the concrete's strength. When a crack forms and water seeps in, it reacts with the lime in the lumps to produce a mineral that gradually fills the crack. In effect, the concrete can repair itself. Experiments indicate that the Romans may have created these lumps deliberately by mixing their materials at very high temperatures.

Engineers are now exploring whether similar techniques could be used in modern construction. If concrete could heal its own cracks, buildings and bridges might last much longer and require fewer repairs. Since producing concrete releases large amounts of carbon dioxide, longer-lasting structures could also help reduce the industry's environmental impact.
Question 1: What did researchers previously believe about the white lumps in Roman concrete?
Question 2: Why are engineers interested in the Roman technique?

questions.q: What did researchers previously believe about the white lumps in Roman concrete?
choices: They indicated that the concrete had been poorly made.
They were added to make the concrete lighter.
They had been created by seawater over time.
They were the main reason for the concrete's strength.
questions.why: For many years … a sign of poor-quality materials or careless mixing＝質の悪さの証拠と思われていた。強さの理由というのは最近の見方で、以前の考えではない。

questions.q: Why are engineers interested in the Roman technique?
choices: It would make concrete cheaper to transport.
It could allow buildings to be constructed more quickly.
It would eliminate the need for lime in concrete.
It might allow modern structures to last longer with fewer repairs.
questions.why: ひびを自分で直せれば建物や橋が長持ちし、修理も減り、二酸化炭素も減らせる。運送費・工期・石灰をなくす、は話に出ない。

sets.script:
As laptops and tablets have become common in classrooms, many students now take notes by typing rather than writing by hand. Typing is faster, and it allows students to record a lecture almost word for word. Surprisingly, however, several studies suggest that this speed may come at a cost.

In a typical experiment, students watched a recorded lecture and took notes either on a laptop or with pen and paper. Afterward, they answered questions about the content. On questions that simply required them to recall facts, the two groups performed similarly. On questions that required them to understand and apply the main ideas, however, the students who had written by hand tended to do better. Researchers believe the reason is that handwriting is slow. Because students cannot write down everything, they are forced to listen carefully, decide what is important, and summarize it in their own words, a process that strengthens understanding.

Not all researchers agree with these findings. Some later studies have found smaller differences or none at all, and critics note that students can be trained to type summaries rather than copying everything. Still, many teachers now encourage students to put their laptops away during at least part of each lesson.
Question 1: According to the speaker, why might handwriting help students understand lectures?
Question 2: What do critics of these findings point out?

questions.q: According to the speaker, why might handwriting help students understand lectures?
choices: It allows them to record every word the lecturer says.
It requires them to select and summarize key points.
It prevents them from becoming distracted by the internet.
It makes it easier for them to read their notes later.
questions.why: 手書きは遅いので全部は書けず、大事な点を選び自分の言葉でまとめる → 理解が深まる。全部書き取れるのはタイピングの方。ネットの誘惑・読み返しやすさは話に出ない。

questions.q: What do critics of these findings point out?
choices: Students could learn to type in a way that involves summarizing.
Handwritten notes are usually much harder to read.
Laptops help students remember facts more accurately.
Most teachers have stopped allowing laptops in class.
questions.why: critics note that students can be trained to type summaries＝要約しながら打つよう訓練できる。事実の記憶はどちらも同じだった。先生の話は最後の「一部の時間しまわせる」だけ。

sets.script:
Honeybees are famous for their "waggle dance," a series of movements that a worker bee performs inside the hive after discovering a good source of food. By waggling her body while moving in a straight line, she communicates both the direction of the food relative to the sun and its distance from the hive. Other bees then use this information to fly directly to the flowers.

For decades, scientists assumed that the dance was entirely instinctive, meaning that bees were born knowing how to perform it. A recent study, however, suggests that learning also plays an important role. Researchers raised groups of young bees in colonies where they could not observe older bees dancing. When these bees eventually began to dance, their movements were noticeably less precise, and they made more errors in signaling distance than bees that had grown up watching experienced dancers.

Interestingly, the inexperienced bees did improve with practice, but some of their errors in communicating distance never fully disappeared. The researchers concluded that, much like human language, the waggle dance depends on a combination of inborn ability and social learning. The findings have led some scientists to wonder how many other animal behaviors once thought to be purely instinctive are in fact partly learned.
Question 1: What information does the waggle dance communicate?
Question 2: What did the study find about bees raised without older dancers?

questions.q: What information does the waggle dance communicate?
choices: Which bees in the hive are the most experienced.
How much food the hive has stored for winter.
Where food is located and how far away it is.
Whether the flowers are safe from predators.
questions.why: 太陽に対する食べ物の方向と巣からの距離を伝える。経験・貯蔵量・安全性は伝えていない。

questions.q: What did the study find about bees raised without older dancers?
choices: They were completely unable to perform the dance.
Their dances contained more mistakes, some of which never disappeared.
They danced more accurately than other bees after practice.
They learned the dance by watching bees from other colonies.
questions.why: 動きが不正確で、練習で良くなったが距離の誤りの一部は消えなかった。踊れなかったわけではない。他より正確になった、は逆。他の巣の蜂を見る話は無い。

sets.script:
Imagine a coffee shop that sells a small coffee for three dollars and a large one for five. Many customers choose the small size. Now suppose the shop adds a medium coffee priced at four dollars and eighty cents. Suddenly, a much larger proportion of customers choose the large size. The medium option is rarely purchased, but its presence changes customers' decisions. Economists and psychologists call this the "decoy effect."

The effect works because people often find it difficult to judge whether a price is reasonable in isolation. Instead, they evaluate options by comparing them with one another. When the large coffee costs only twenty cents more than the medium, it suddenly appears to be a bargain, even though its price has not changed at all. Businesses ranging from cinemas to software companies use similar strategies to guide customers toward more expensive products.

Some researchers, however, argue that the decoy effect is weaker in real life than in laboratory experiments. When people are familiar with a product or have a clear idea of what they want, they are less easily influenced by an extra option. Nevertheless, understanding the effect can help consumers recognize when their choices are being shaped by the way options are presented.
Question 1: Why does adding a medium-sized coffee increase sales of the large size?
Question 2: According to some researchers, when is the decoy effect weaker?

questions.q: Why does adding a medium-sized coffee increase sales of the large size?
choices: It makes the large size seem like good value by comparison.
It lowers the price that customers pay for the large size.
It reduces the number of small coffees the shop can sell.
It gives customers more time to decide what they want.
questions.why: 中サイズより20セント高いだけなので、大サイズがお得に見える（比べて判断する）。大サイズの値段は変わっていない。

questions.q: According to some researchers, when is the decoy effect weaker?
choices: When businesses offer more than three options.
When customers are shopping at a cinema.
When people already know a product well or know what they want.
When the decoy option is the cheapest one available.
questions.why: When people are familiar with a product or have a clear idea of what they want＝よく知っている・欲しい物がはっきりしている時。選択肢の数・映画館・最安の囮、は話に出ない。

sets.script: Hi, this is Gloria from Westside Auto, calling about your car. We've finished the inspection, and the main problem is the brake pads, which are badly worn. We can replace them for $380, and that job can be done by Thursday afternoon. We also noticed that the timing belt is close to the end of its life. Replacing it would cost another $450. It's not urgent, but we'd recommend doing it within the next three months. If you'd like us to do both jobs now, we'd need to order the belt, and the car wouldn't be ready until Monday. Alternatively, you could have the brakes done this week and come back for the belt another time. Just give me a call back and let me know which option you prefer. If we don't hear from you by noon tomorrow, we won't be able to finish anything by Thursday.

questions.q:
Situation: You need your car for a business trip on Friday morning. You can spend up to $600 on repairs. You receive this voicemail from the repair shop.
Question: What should you do?
choices: Call the shop by noon tomorrow and ask for only the brakes to be replaced.
Ask the shop to replace both the brakes and the timing belt now.

sets.script:
W: Today I'm talking with Dr. Owen Brooks, a sleep researcher who has spent the last fifteen years studying teenagers. Dr. Brooks, thank you for joining us.
M: It's my pleasure. It's a topic that matters to almost every family with teenage children.
W: Let's start with a basic question. Why do teenagers seem to have so much trouble getting up in the morning?
M: Well, many parents assume it's simply laziness or staying up too late on their phones. Those things can certainly make the problem worse. But the main cause is biological. During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts. The hormone that makes us feel sleepy, melatonin, starts to be released later in the evening. So a typical sixteen-year-old may not feel tired until eleven or even midnight, no matter how early they go to bed.
W: But they still have to get up for school.
M: Exactly, and that's the heart of the problem. Most teenagers need around eight to ten hours of sleep. If they can't fall asleep until midnight and have to be up at six thirty, they're losing several hours every night. Over a week, that adds up to a serious sleep deficit.
W: What are the consequences of that?
M: They're more wide-ranging than people realize. The obvious one is difficulty concentrating in class, especially in the first few periods. But chronic lack of sleep also affects mood. Sleep-deprived teenagers are more likely to feel irritable and anxious, and they find it harder to control their emotions. There's also evidence that it increases the risk of accidents, particularly among young drivers.
W: Do teenagers themselves realize they're not getting enough sleep?
M: Often not. Many of them have been tired for so long that they think it's normal. When we ask students to keep sleep diaries for two weeks, they're frequently shocked by how little they actually sleep.
W: Some schools have responded by starting classes later. Has that made a difference?
M: In the schools we've studied, yes. When one district moved its starting time from seven forty-five to eight thirty, students got on average about forty minutes more sleep per night. Attendance improved, and teachers reported that students were more alert. That said, changing school schedules isn't easy. It affects bus routes, after-school sports, and parents' work schedules, so there's often resistance.
W: What about families? Is there anything parents can do?
M: Quite a lot, actually. The most important thing is consistency. Teenagers often sleep until noon on weekends to make up for lost sleep, but that shifts their internal clock even later and makes Monday mornings worse. I'd recommend that they get up no more than an hour or two later on weekends than on school days. Getting bright light in the morning helps too, as it signals to the brain that the day has started.
W: And what about screens? Should parents ban phones in the bedroom?
M: I'm generally not in favor of strict bans, because they tend to lead to conflict and teenagers find ways around them. What seems to work better is agreeing on a time, perhaps an hour before bed, when devices go onto a charger in the kitchen. The light from screens isn't the only issue. Messages and videos keep the brain active and alert when it should be winding down. If parents follow the same rule themselves, teenagers are much more likely to accept it.
W: Dr. Brooks, thank you so much for your insights.
M: Thank you for having me.

sets.script:
M: My guest today is Akiko Lindqvist, who works as a video game translator. Akiko, welcome to the program.
W: Thanks, it's great to be here.
M: How did you get into this line of work? It's not exactly a career most people plan for.
W: No, definitely not. I studied literature at university, and I was planning to translate novels. But while I was a student, I took a part-time job testing games for a small studio. My job was just to find bugs, but I kept noticing that the English text in the Japanese games was awkward, sometimes even incomprehensible. I started sending suggestions to the producer, and eventually she asked me to rewrite all the dialogue for one of their games. That was twelve years ago, and I've been doing it ever since.
M: What makes translating games different from translating books?
W: In many ways, it's more technical. With a novel, you have the whole text in front of you, in order. With a game, you often receive thousands of separate lines in a spreadsheet, with no pictures and very little context. A single word like "fire" could be a command to shoot, a type of magic, or an item on a menu, and if you guess wrong, it can confuse players. There are also strict space limits. If a line in a menu can only hold twelve characters, I have to find a way to say everything within those twelve characters.
M: I imagine humor is especially difficult.
W: It's the hardest part, and also my favorite. Jokes in games often depend on wordplay, or on references to television shows or local customs that players in another country wouldn't recognize. If I translated them literally, the joke would disappear. So instead, I try to understand what the scene is supposed to achieve. Is the character supposed to seem clumsy, or arrogant, or kind? Then I write a new joke that creates the same effect for an English-speaking player. Sometimes the new joke has nothing in common with the original except the feeling it creates.
M: Do the original creators mind when you change things that much?
W: Some are nervous at first. But most of the game directors I work with understand that a literal translation can actually be less faithful, because players won't react the way the creators intended. I always explain my changes and why I made them. Building that trust is a big part of the job.
M: What was the most challenging project you've worked on?
W: Probably a fantasy game in which one group of characters spoke an invented language. The creators had made up hundreds of words, and I had to keep them consistent across more than half a million words of text. I ended up building my own dictionary just to keep track.
M: How do you see the field changing? Many people are talking about machine translation.
W: Machine translation is already useful for things like technical descriptions or very repetitive text, and it saves us time. But I don't think it can handle the creative side yet. A machine can translate the words of a joke, but it doesn't know whether players will laugh. I suspect my job will shift toward editing and reviewing machine output for routine text, while human translators focus more on characters and story.
M: Any advice for people who want to follow in your footsteps?
W: Play lots of games, obviously, but also read widely in your own language. People often think the most important skill is knowing the foreign language, but in my experience, the hardest part is writing natural, lively dialogue in your native language.
M: Akiko, thank you very much.

Question 2: What does Akiko say about translating humor?
